description: Editorial description of the on-screen teaching sequence; not spoken narration. The soundtrack is music.

segments.text: Text preparation turns a sequence of symbols into vectors that the Transformer can process.
The teaching example uses Tiny Shakespeare and compares different choices of token unit.
Word tokenization uses whole words, but creates a larger vocabulary and needs a policy for unseen words.
Subword tokenization can represent words using reusable pieces.
Byte-pair encoding repeatedly merges frequent neighboring units, using rules learned from the training text.
The Shakespeare example illustrates a learned BPE vocabulary and its effect on sequence length.
The reference comparison uses 65 character tokens, 12,571 word entries or 265 BPE entries. Counts depend on the tokenizer and split.
Larger vocabularies increase the embedding table and output vocabulary projection. The character table here has 65×64 = 4,160 entries.
An ID selects one row from the embedding table. This converts each token into a 64-dimensional starting vector.
Position information distinguishes identical tokens at different locations. This model learns 64 position vectors of width 64.
Split training and validation text before making windows, preventing windows from crossing the split and leaking validation text.
The input is a text window. The target is the same stream shifted one token ahead, so each position predicts its successor.
A batch groups 32 windows of 64 token IDs. Input and target tensors have shape 32×64 before embedding.
Pause: why split before sampling windows? What grows when vocabulary size grows?
Splitting first keeps validation content out of training. Both the embedding table and output projection grow with vocabulary size.
Recap: tokenize, look up vectors, include positions, split carefully, and create shifted input–target windows.
